newsitem.title: UK: British gilts face rising political risk.
newsitem.headline: British gilts face rising political risk.

text.p: Gilts have made impressive gains in recent weeks but some analysts say political risk will return to dog the market, despite soothing rhetoric from Britain's two main election rivals.
While the spread between gilt and German Bund yields has narrowed to some 150 basis points, the risk over the medium-term is for that gap to widen to around 200 as gilts underperform.
"The political risk premium in gilts is naive -- it is just too small," Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in London, said on Friday.
"The bottom line is -- sell gilts if we get below 150 basis points (on the spread)."
Analysts said that despite slick performances and a show of unity from both Labour and ruling Consevative Party conferences, investors should beware of taking the speeches at face value.

"We saw a masterful political performance by the Chancellor (of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke). But it was a classic Tory conference speech and had only a miniscule amount of policy in it," said Richardson.
"And all Labour have come up with is a lot of bland policy statements -- none of which has any meat on the bone."

With most opinion polls putting the Labour Party at least 20 points ahead of the Conservatives and a general election due by May 1997, gilts have been relatively sanguine about the prospect of a left-of-centre government, believing the old tax-and-spend party has changed its approach.
David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC investment bank in London, said this was a risky stance.
"The problem for Labour is that their economic policies in particular are still very much an unknown quantity," he said.
"We may just see a panic in the gilt market before the election because there will be worries that maybe Labour hasn't changed after all," he said.

But others said a general perception that a Labour election win would bring Britain closer to joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- ensuring that fiscal reins are kept tight and inflation under control -- will boost gilt prices.
Officially, neither of Britain's main political parties has said whether or not it will join a single currency.
"The overriding bullish scenario for the gilt market would be a majority Labour win," said David Owen, UK economist at Kleinwort Benson in London.

"There is absolutely no chance that (Labour leader) Tony Blair or (shadow chancellor) Gordon Brown will make a committment to EMU this side of election -- there is no political upside in that," he said. "But the markets know there is a much higher chance that Labour will take the UK into EMU than the Tories."

While investors buying bonds in France, Spain, Italy and Sweden, among others, have made a killing on EMU convergence plays with yield spreads between Bunds and other European bonds tightening dramatically in recent months, gilts have been left out of the party so far.

But Owen said a growing belief that a Labour government would pull Britain into a single European currency will encourage similar convergence trades between Britain and Germany and advised buying gilts. Yamaichi's Richardson disagreed.

He noted that both the Labour and Conservative parties have pledged to put the EMU issue to the people -- either in the form of a referendum or a general election -- and said this meant the chance of Britain participating in the euro was distant.
"The bottom line is that we're going to have a referendum on EMU -- and opinion polls show now that if you have a referendum you're going to get a "no' vote," he said.
"We might be able to meet the Maastricht criteria -- but because of public opinion the issue is academic."
